questions.q: In the unstructured search problem, what is f allowed to be, and what can an algorithm do with it?
options: f is a hash function, and the algorithm may inspect its internal hash buckets directly
f is any function, but the algorithm is told its full source code in advance
f is always a sorted array, and the algorithm may use binary search on it
f is an opaque oracle mapping each input to 0 or 1; the algorithm may only query it on an input and read back the output, with no access to how it's computed
questions.explain: The oracle model strips away all structure and internal visibility: the algorithm can call f(x) and get 0 or 1 back, nothing else, which is exactly what makes the problem 'unstructured.'

questions.q: What is the classical worst-case number of oracle queries needed to find the one marked item among N, with no structure to exploit?
options: √N queries
Up to N queries, since any unqueried input is indistinguishable from any other until it's actually checked
log2(N) queries, via binary search
A constant number of queries regardless of N
questions.explain: Without structure, two unqueried inputs look identical to the algorithm, so in the worst case the marked item could be the very last one checked -- up to N queries.

questions.q: What is the classical average-case number of queries needed, averaged over all possible positions of the marked item?
options: N/2 queries
N queries, same as the worst case
log2(N) queries on average
1 query on average
questions.explain: Averaging uniformly over where the marked item could sit among N positions gives an expected N/2 queries before finding it.

questions.q: Why doesn't a hash table or B-tree index solve the unstructured search problem in O(1) or O(log N) time?
options: Because N must be prime for a hash table to work
Because those techniques rely on exploitable structure (sorted order, precomputed hash buckets) that, by definition, doesn't exist in the unstructured case -- they solve a different, easier problem
Because they require quantum hardware to function at all
Because hash tables and B-trees are theoretical constructs that don't actually work in practice
questions.explain: Hash tables and B-trees get their speed from structure imposed on or discovered in the data ahead of time. Unstructured search is specifically the case where no such structure exists to exploit.

questions.q: Roughly how many oracle checks would a billion-record unstructured search need in the worst case, classically, and what is this chapter building toward as an alternative?
options: Up to a billion checks classically; the chapter builds toward a quantum algorithm (Grover's) needing roughly the square root of that, around tens of thousands of oracle calls
A billion checks classically, and no algorithm -- classical or quantum -- can do better
The number of checks needed has nothing to do with the size of the dataset
One single check, since a billion-record database always has an index available
questions.explain: The classical bound is O(N) queries -- up to a billion for a billion records. This chapter is building toward Grover's algorithm, which achieves O(√N) oracle calls on the identical unstructured problem.
